title: Thanthai Periyar and Rajaji: Fierce Ideological Foes, Lifelong Cherished Friends
summary: Though standing on polar opposite sides of ideology and social politics, Thanthai Periyar and C. Rajagopalachari shared a half-century of pure, unbreakable personal friendship.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 161: நேருவின் விடுமுறை: மாதாந்திர செய்தியாளர் சந்திப்பு
full_text:
Throughout the mid-twentieth century, Tamil Nadu’s intellectual landscape was dominated by two titanic figures who occupied diametrically opposed ideological universes: Periyar E. V. Ramasamy and Chakravarti Rajagopalachari (Rajaji).

Periyar was a staunch rationalist, anti-caste iconoclast, and champion of social justice; Rajaji was a deeply religious scholar, classical conservative, and founding patron of the Swatantra Party. On public platforms, their debates were uncompromising and relentless, dissecting each other's ideas with lethal precision.

Yet behind the public gladiatorship lay fifty years of profound, unconditional personal friendship that stunned observers.

In the late 1960s, when Rajaji was hospitalized in Chennai with severe illness, the nonagenarian Periyar—himself frail and confined to a wheelchair—rushed to the hospital in deep distress.

Sitting by the hospital bed, Periyar grasped Rajaji’s hands, tears rolling down his weathered cheeks. Rajaji smiled weakly and whispered with trademark wit:
"Look at you, Ramasamy! On the public platform you assail my politics with thunder, yet here you sit weeping over my bed!"

Periyar replied with raw, emotional candor:
"Rajaji, I sharpen my intellect against your brilliance. Where in this entire country will I find an ideological adversary as honorable, as honest, and as worthy of battle as you? If you leave, with whom shall I debate? Your life is precious to me!"

When Rajaji passed away in December 1972, the grief-stricken Periyar sat beside his mortal remains for hours, weeping openly. Their relationship remains an enduring lesson for democracies: political disagreement must never poison personal love and human decency.
